evidence.text: Lipid nanoparticle encapsulating messenger RNA (LNP-mRNA) has emerged as a promising tool for therapeutic gene delivery in applications such as in vivo chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell production and in vivo hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) gene editing.1,2,3 However, despite the tremendous success of LNP-mRNA technology for vaccine applications, this system still faces challenges in achieving sufficient dosages for extrahepatic applications in vivo, largely due to the innate immune response and phagocytic uptake of LNP-mRNA by cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (MPS).4 Furthermore, while LNP-mRNA are still in the bloodstream, they naturally bind to serum proteins such as apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to form a protein corona, which promotes their uptake by the liver hepatocytes through the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) classical pathway.5,6 Although beneficial for hepatic delivery of therapeutics,7,8 this liver tropism poses a challenge for efficient delivery of LNP-mRNA therapies to non-liver cells in vivo.

evidence.text: Following delivery into the bloodstream, the protein corona forms around the LNPs, allowing for increased uptake by the MPS and subsequent processing in the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.9 The MPS consists of immune surveillance cells such as monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, which engulf bacteria, dead tissue cells, and exogenous material.

MPS cells widely express the phagocytosis regulatory marker, signal regulatory protein-α (SIRP-α) on their surface.10 The anti-phagocytic counterpart of SIRP-α is transmembrane protein CD47, which is a recognition molecule acting as a ubiquitous “don’t eat me” signal found on cell surfaces.10
